summary: A Network Host Status report covering June 5 to June 16, 1972. The MIT Math Lab PDP-10 became a server. No testing was done on June 6 because of an attempt to install the new IMP system, or on June 9 because the prototype Terminal IMP was used for debugging. It was replaced by RFC 366.

plainLanguage.summary: This is like a school attendance sheet for the early internet. Someone wrote down which big computers were switched on and ready to help, and which ones were not, so people knew where to go.

subtitle: Checking which network hosts were working in June 1972

tldr.problem: Users needed current status of ARPANET host availability.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested network hosts from June 5 to June 16, 1972. The MIT Math Lab PDP-10 (Address 198) became a server during this period.
tldr.outcome: The report shows continued network growth. MIT expanded its ARPANET resources by adding a fourth PDP-10 for the Mathematics Laboratory.

today: RFC 366 replaced this status report in July 1972. These early status reports documented ARPANET's rapid growth during its critical formative period.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 362 reports on host status from June 5 to June 16, 1972. During this period, the MIT Math Lab PDP-10 (Address 198) became a network server. No testing was done on June 6 due to an attempt to install the new IMP system, and no testing occurred on June 9 because the prototype Terminal IMP was being used for software debugging. On June 16, the ARPA Terminal IMP (Address 156) was installed in Arlington, Virginia.
sections.plainLanguage: MIT's mathematics researchers got their own computer connected to the network. The ARPANET team continued upgrading the network's core switching systems.

sections.title: Network Expansion
sections.content:
The Terminal IMP count continued growing, with Terminal IMPs at AMES, MITRE, NBS, ETAC, USC, GWC, NOAA, RADC, SAAC, BELVOIR, ARPA, and BBN now excluded from daily testing. The operational server list now included the MIT Math Lab in addition to three other MIT systems (Multics, DM, and AI). This showed MIT's heavy investment in the ARPANET.

The expanding Terminal IMP network allowed smaller organizations and government agencies to connect without maintaining large dedicated computer systems, democratizing ARPANET access.
sections.plainLanguage: More and more organizations got Terminal IMPs to connect to the network. MIT had four different computers available to the network now. The network was reaching beyond just the big universities.

sections.title: Host Status and Reliability
sections.content:
The testing results show typical reliability patterns. Most major servers like UCLA, SRI-NIC, UCSB, MIT-Multics, RAND CSG, and Harvard-10 achieved Open status on most days. The new MIT Math Lab server showed significant connection problems (mostly Half Open), as was typical for newly connected systems.

Some machines continued to show persistent failures. AMES-67 and SDC-ADEPT were dead almost every day. SRI-AI, which had been dead for months, remained inaccessible. These chronic failures represented either outdated systems, local site issues, or fundamental incompatibilities with the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Most computers worked pretty well. MIT's new computer had some trouble at first connecting. A couple of computers were broken almost the whole time, which had been going on for weeks.
